## Pearson Correlation {.smaller}

<img style="float:left; width:150px; margin:0 20px 20px 0px;" src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/18/Karl_Pearson%2C_1912.jpg">

In statistics, the Pearson correlation coefficient, also referred to as the Pearson's r, Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient (PPMCC) or bivariate correlation, is a measure of the linear correlation between two variables X and Y. It has a value between +1 and −1, where 1 is total positive linear correlation, 0 is no linear correlation, and −1 is total negative linear correlation. It is widely used in the sciences. It was developed by Karl Pearson from a related idea introduced by Francis Galton in the 1880s.

Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson_correlation_coefficient)

## Pearson Correlation

$$r_{xy} = \frac{{COV}_{xy}}{S_xS_y}$$
Where $S$ is the standard deviation and $COV$ is the covariance.

$${COV}_{xy} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{N-1}$$

## Plot correlation

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.width=5, fig.height=5, fig.align='center'}
data <- read.csv(datasetsPath("2026/exam-anxiety.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
# five students picked so that no two share a value and all four quadrants are used
tinydat <- data[c(95, 50, 77, 54, 94), ]
x <- tinydat$`Exam anxiety`
y <- tinydat$`Exam performance`
myLimsX <- c(68, 91)
myLimsY <- c(10, 95)
plot(x, y, las = 1, xlab = "Anxiety", ylab = "Exam performance (%)", 
     xlim = myLimsX, ylim = myLimsY)

m.x <- mean(x)
m.y <- mean(y)


points(x,y, pch = 21, bg = "turquoise", col = "black", lwd = 2, cex = 1.5)
corners <- par("usr")


```

## Load data

```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=TRUE}
data <- read.csv(datasetsPath("2026/exam-anxiety.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
data <- data[, c("Time spent revising", "Exam performance", "Exam anxiety")]
ssrTable(data)
```

```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
exam_grade   <- data$`Exam performance`
anxiety      <- data$`Exam anxiety`
N            <- length(exam_grade)
mean.exam    <- mean(exam_grade)
mean.anxiety <- mean(anxiety)
z.exam       <- (exam_grade - mean(exam_grade)) / sd(exam_grade)
z.anxiety    <- (anxiety    - mean(anxiety))    / sd(anxiety)
```

## Covariance {.subsection}

$${COV}_{xy} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{N-1}$$

```{r, echo=TRUE}
mean.exam    <- mean(exam_grade, na.rm=TRUE)
mean.anxiety <- mean(anxiety,    na.rm=TRUE)

delta.exam    <- exam_grade - mean.exam
delta.anxiety <- anxiety    - mean.anxiety

prod <- delta.exam * delta.anxiety

covariance <- sum(prod) / (N - 1)
covariance
```

## Correlation

$$r_{xy} = \frac{{COV}_{xy}}{S_xS_y}$$

```{r, echo=TRUE}
correlation <- covariance / ( sd(exam_grade) * sd(anxiety) ); correlation
```

## Correlation
$$r_{xy} = \frac{{COV}_{xy}}{S_xS_y}$$
$${COV}_{xy} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{N-1}$$


```{r, echo=TRUE}
cor(exam_grade, anxiety) # correlation

cor(z.exam,     z.anxiety) # correlation of z-scores
```

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# covariance of z-scores
sum(z.exam * z.anxiety ) / (N - 1)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
xBot <- corners[1]
yTop <- corners[4]
yBot <- corners[3]
polygon(c(mean.anxiety,xTop,xTop,mean.anxiety),c(mean.exam,mean.exam,yTop,yTop), col = rgb(0,0.8,0,.2))
polygon(c(mean.anxiety,xBot,xBot,mean.anxiety),c(mean.exam,mean.exam,yBot,yBot), col = rgb(0,0.8,0,.2))

polygon(c(mean.anxiety,xBot,xBot,mean.anxiety),c(mean.exam,mean.exam,yTop,yTop), col = rgb(0.8,0,0,alpha = 0.2))
polygon(c(mean.anxiety,xTop,xTop,mean.anxiety),c(mean.exam,mean.exam,yBot,yBot), col = rgb(0.8,0,0,alpha= 0.2))

# x is anxiety, y is exam performance
xMargin <- 6
yMargin <- 12
text(mean.anxiety+xMargin, mean.exam+yMargin, "+ * +", cex = 2, col = "red")
text(mean.anxiety-xMargin, mean.exam-yMargin, "- * -", cex = 2, col = "red")
text(mean.anxiety+xMargin, mean.exam-yMargin, "+ * -", cex = 2, col = "red")
text(mean.anxiety-xMargin, mean.exam+yMargin, "- * +", cex = 2, col = "red")
```

## Significance testing using $t$

> A test statistic with a known probability distribution (the t-distribution).

It's a standardized measure of how closely our observed statistic matches the value claimed by $H_0$:

$$t = \frac{\text{estimate} - H_0 \text{ value}}{\text{SE}(\text{estimate})}$$

## Significance of a correlation {.subsection}

> We convert $r$ to a $t$-statistic because $t$ has a sampling distribution: the $t$-distribution with df = N-2:

$$t_r = \frac{r \sqrt{N-2}}{\sqrt{1 - r^2}}$$

$${df} = N - 2$$

## Hypotheses for $t$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_0 &: t_r = 0 \\
H_A &: t_r \neq 0 \\
H_A &: t_r > 0 \\
H_A &: t_r < 0 \\
\end{aligned}
$$

## $r$  to $t$ 

```{r, echo=TRUE}
df  <- N-2
t.r <- ( correlation*sqrt(df) ) / sqrt(1-correlation^2)

t.r
df
```

## One-sided vs two-sided {.smaller}

The hypotheses above translate into where we shade the rejection region:

[Additional text here](https://johnnydoorn.github.io/teaching-statistics/extra-texts/one-sided-vs-two-sided.html)

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.6}
layout(matrix(1:2, 1, 2))
par(cex = 0.8, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.main = 1.2)

tCurve(df, alpha = .05, sided = "two",
       main = bquote("Two-sided: reject when |t| >" ~ .(round(qt(.975, df), 2))))

tCurve(df, alpha = .05, sided = "right",
       main = bquote("One-sided: reject when t >" ~ .(round(qt(.95, df), 2))))
```

Same $\alpha$, split over two tails or spent on one.

## Visualize

Locate in $t$-distribution

```{r, echo=FALSE}
tCurve(df, sided = "two", observed = t.r, showRegion = FALSE,
       main = "Our observed t in the null distribution")

p.r <- 2 * pt(abs(t.r), df, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

$$P(|t| \geq `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(t.r))` \mid H_0) `r if (p.r < .001) "< .001" else sprintf("= %.3f", p.r)`$$
